title: Content-level deduplication at ingest time
detail: PiyAPI silently merges records with identical content text. Records 3 and 2 of our micro batch both say 'Morgan Vale's preferred database is PostgreSQL' (one is the 2024-06 superseded version, one is the 2025-11 active version). PiyAPI returned the same ID (88338532) for both — only the first-ingested version survives. Similarly, our intentional duplicate pair (records 8 and 9) collapsed into one ID (b26a2d57). This means: (a) the system cannot distinguish superseded vs active records with identical text, (b) metadata from the second ingest may be silently dropped, (c) our 10-record batch became 8 stored records.

title: Deduplication keeps first-ingested metadata, discards second
detail: When two records with identical text are ingested, the PiyAPI-assigned ID matches the first record. The metadata from the second POST (which had status=active, timestamp=2025-11-03 for the PostgreSQL preference) was discarded. The surviving record has status=superseded, timestamp=2024-06-15. This means the current/active version was lost in favor of the older superseded version — the opposite of correct temporal behavior.

title: No timestamp-aware ranking in search results
detail: Query: 'What is Morgan Vale's current preferred database?' Top result was the superseded PostgreSQL record (ts=2024-06-15, score=0.868). The word 'current' in the query had no effect on ranking — the system ranked purely by semantic similarity. The SQLite record (ts=2023-02-01) ranked below unrelated records. PiyAPI does not appear to use timestamp or status metadata in its search ranking.
query: What is Morgan Vale's current preferred database?

title: Both sides of a conflict pair are surfaced in search
detail: Query: 'What is Jamie Hart's meeting preference?' Both disputed records appeared in results — 'early meetings' (rank 1, score=0.810) and 'late meetings' (rank 3, score=0.666). A non-meeting-related record ('preferring aisle seat', rank 2, score=0.579) appeared between them. The system does surface competing claims but does not flag them as disputed — it would take an LLM reading the results to notice the contradiction.
query: What is Jamie Hart's meeting preference?

title: No abstention on unanswerable queries — always returns results
detail: Query: 'What is Morgan Vale's favorite color?' (not in corpus). The system returned 5 results with the top score=0.871 (the PostgreSQL preference record). The system has no concept of 'I don't know' — it always returns the top-k nearest neighbors regardless of whether they're actually relevant. The highest-scoring result is completely unrelated to the query topic. An LLM consuming these results would likely hallucinate an answer.
query: What is Morgan Vale's favorite color?

title: Alias resolution works through semantic similarity but not alias metadata
detail: Query: 'What is Project Atlas?' Both Atlas records appeared in results (rank 1 and 2, scores 0.859 and 0.753). However, this is pure semantic match on the word 'Atlas' — the aliases field (['Project Atlas', 'atlas-svc']) stored in metadata was not used for resolution. The system would likely fail on a query using 'atlas-svc' or 'atlas-core' alone.

title: Alias metadata is stored but not indexed for search
detail: Confirmed via three queries: (1) 'atlas-svc' — this alias appears in metadata.aliases on the Acme Robotics record but not the Rust record. Both returned at similar scores (0.780 vs 0.719), meaning the alias metadata provided no boost. (2) 'atlas-core' — does NOT appear in ANY metadata. Yet returned nearly identical scores (0.779, 0.740) to the atlas-svc query. This proves all matching is purely content-semantic. (3) 'M. Vale preferred database' — resolved to Morgan Vale at score 0.865, but this is embedding similarity between 'M. Vale' and 'Morgan Vale' in the content text, not alias resolution. PiyAPI stores custom metadata faithfully but does not use it for search relevance.

title: Dedup metadata survival confirmed; version bump inconsistent
detail: Verified via GET on both deduplicated pairs: (1) PostgreSQL pair: first-ingested metadata survived completely (corpus_id=e13ad2e1, status=superseded, timestamp=2024-06-15). Second ingest's metadata (status=active, timestamp=2025-11-03) was silently dropped. PiyAPI version=2, suggesting the system acknowledged the dedup collision but chose not to update metadata. (2) Aisle seat pair: first-ingested metadata survived (corpus_id=e7ff1089). But PiyAPI version=1 — no version bump. The inconsistency (version=2 vs version=1) between the two dedup events is unexplained. Practical implication: you cannot rely on dedup to merge or update records — it silently discards the newer submission while sometimes incrementing a version counter.

title: Cross-record version bumps when related content is ingested
detail: After ingesting batch 2 (10 new records), existing records had their version numbers changed WITHOUT being re-ingested: PostgreSQL preference went from v2 to v3, SQLite preference is now v2. Additionally, freshly ingested records started at v2 instead of v1: MongoDB (v2), Docker (v2), Podman (v2). PiyAPI appears to run cross-record analysis (possibly contradiction detection, as suggested by 'processing_status: checking_contradictions' and 'contradiction_detected' fields on records) that bumps version numbers on related records. The version field does NOT simply count how many times a record was written — it reflects some internal processing state.

title: Hybrid search results not sorted by hybridScore — importance/confidence boost
detail: search/hybrid results are NOT sorted by hybridScore. The actual ranking uses a compound formula that boosts records with higher PiyAPI-assigned importance_score and confidence_score. Example: Atlas 'Acme Robotics' (hybridScore=0.731, imp=0.5, conf=0.65) ranked above Docker (hybridScore=0.821, imp=0.3, conf=0.3). The exact formula is opaque — it's NOT a simple linear combination (tested multiple weight hypotheses, none fit all data points). Practical impact: result[0] is NOT necessarily the most semantically similar result, and a client cannot reproduce the ranking from visible score fields alone. Note: POST /search (semantic-only) DOES sort correctly by similarity. The boost is specific to search/hybrid.

title: Search index lags behind primary store after cross-record processing
detail: Records that undergo cross-record version bumps (triggered by ingesting related/conflicting content) show stale data in search results: version=0, null confidence_score, and possibly corrupted embedding vectors. GET returns the correct current values. Confirmed on 4 records: PostgreSQL (GET v3, search v0), SQLite (GET v2, search v0), Podman (GET v2, search v0), proj-atl (GET v1, search inconsistent). The lag persisted for at least the duration of our testing session (~10 minutes after batch 2 ingest). Implication: search results immediately after bulk ingestion may return stale or incorrect metadata and ranking for records that were modified by the system's background contradiction-detection pipeline.

title: Stale-index records get anomalously high hybridScores but are deprioritized
detail: Records with version=0 (stale search index) sometimes receive impossibly high hybridScores — e.g., PostgreSQL preference scored 0.930 for a 'Jamie Hart meetings' query (semanticScore=0.738, bm25=0). The hybridScore formula appears to produce inflated scores for unprocessed records. However, PiyAPI pushes these records to the END of results regardless of score — they consistently appear in the tail positions. This suggests a two-phase ranking: (1) processed records ranked by compound score (hybridScore + importance/confidence boost), (2) unprocessed/stale records appended after, regardless of their hybridScore. The result is that stale records don't pollute the top-k, but their inflated scores are misleading if consumed by position-unaware clients.

title: GET /memories pagination broken: page param cycles, after param overlaps
detail: The 'page' query parameter for GET /memories does not advance — every page value (1 through 9) returns the same 100 records. The 'after' cursor parameter also fails, returning overlapping results. Only the 'offset' parameter works correctly for enumerating records beyond the first 100. With 118 records in the namespace, only offset-based pagination (offset=0 → 100 records, offset=100 → 18 records) retrieves them all. The default listing caps at 100 records and returns the most-recently-created records, so older records are invisible without explicit offset. This is a significant usability bug for any client that needs to enumerate a namespace.

title: Signal dilution at scale: relevant records buried by noise above ~100 records
detail: At 18 records (R009/R014), the Morgan Vale DB preference query found MongoDB at rank 1 and relevant results dominated. At 118 records (R019), none of the 3 DB preference records appeared in the top 5 — they were displaced by semantically adjacent but irrelevant records (migration checklists, meeting preferences, malformed corpus records). Similarly, 'atlas-svc' went from finding both Atlas records (R010) to finding only 1 of 6+ Atlas records in top 5. The search/hybrid endpoint returns only 10 results (total_candidates=10), meaning it performs an early cutoff before the importance/confidence reranking, which further shuffles relevant results out of the top positions. At scale, the combination of (a) 10-candidate limit, (b) pure semantic similarity without metadata filtering, and (c) importance/confidence reranking makes it unreliable for precise fact retrieval.

title: Abstention threshold too permissive at 0.6 — fails on name-matching nonsense queries
detail: Query: 'What is Riley Chen's shoe size?' (not in corpus, unanswerable). abstain=false because top_similarity=0.640 exceeds abstain_threshold=0.600. The system found Riley Chen records (migration checklists, preferences) that are completely irrelevant to shoe size but score above threshold because the person's name matches. This means the abstention mechanism only triggers when the query shares zero semantic overlap with any stored content — not when the query topic is absent. Any query mentioning a known entity will pass the threshold regardless of whether the predicate is answerable. This makes abstention nearly useless for real-world 'I don't know' scenarios where the entity exists but the fact doesn't.

title: Formal benchmark: 65% pass rate (26/40) masks a structural ceiling
detail: First formal benchmark run against 118-record namespace with 40 runnable test cases (121 skipped due to uningested corpus IDs). Overall 65% pass rate is inflated by two categories that pass by design: exact_duplicate always passes (informational, 10/10), and alias works via semantic content matching (14/14). Removing those, the 'real' pass rate is 2/16 (12.5%) — only uncertainty cases pass. Every capability that requires the system to go beyond raw semantic similarity fails: supersession (0/6, no temporal ranking), abstention (0/5, no 'I don't know'), point_retrieval (0/1, signal dilution at scale), semantic_duplicate (0/2, dilution). The system is fundamentally a semantic nearest-neighbor search with an opaque reranking boost. It stores metadata faithfully but does not use it for search relevance, cannot distinguish current from stale facts, and cannot abstain. An LLM layer on top would need to do all temporal reasoning, conflict resolution, and relevance filtering itself — at which point the memory system is just a vector store with extra fields.

title: Temporal traps: system ranks misleading/false/stale records above correct current truth in 6/6 queries
detail: Against 40 Northstar Array records with carefully labeled truth_role metadata, PiyAPI's hybrid search ranked the correct current_truth answer at rank 1 in ZERO out of 6 queries. Results: (1) 'current scheduler' — misleading_distractor rank 1, correct AURORA rank 4. (2) 'Kestrel migration complete?' — false_claim rank 1, correct 'shelved' rank 3. (3) 'March outage cause' — misleading_distractor rank 1, correct G-17 rank 4. (4) 'shutdown manual or automatic?' — misleading_distractor rank 1, correct 'manual' rank 3. (5) 'site name' — misleading_distractor rank 1, correct 'Nadir Station' rank 3. (6) 'generator-only power?' — stale_truth rank 1, correct 'mixed power' rank 2. One specific record (T026, 'July report refers to March outage at Nadir Station') appeared at rank 1 in 4 of 6 queries — PiyAPI's opaque reranking gave it dominant importance despite being labeled misleading_distractor. The system has no concept of truth_role, recency, or supersession. Any LLM consuming rank-1 results would answer incorrectly 100% of the time.

title: False consensus: majority-volume stale claims overwhelm minority-correct evidence; query phrasing determines whether truth surfaces
detail: Against 40 Nightglass Festival records testing citation cascade (16 records say 18k, 5 say 12.4k), results are query-phrasing-dependent: (1) 'permitted occupancy' — correct 12,400 at rank 1 (fire permit's exact language matches), but still 5 wrong vs 2 correct in top 10. (2) 'South Yard capacity' — correct 12,400 at rank 1 but 18,000 dominates ranks 2-5 (6 wrong vs 2 correct in top 10). (3) 'How many people can it hold?' — WRONG 18,000 at rank 1 (casual phrasing matches cascade documents), correct at rank 5 (6 wrong vs 3 correct in top 10). An LLM doing majority voting, source-counting, or using the 'most common answer' heuristic would be wrong in all three cases. An LLM trusting rank 1 would be wrong for the most natural query phrasing. The water pressure control arc works correctly (genuinely independent observations surface together), confirming the issue is specifically about derived/copied claims inflating volume. Gate assignment arc: correct Gate F at rank 1, but old Gate C still present.

title: Experiment 05: full-corpus hybrid retrieval exposes an incomplete evidence view
detail: With all 202 Experiment 05 records ingested chronologically and all oracle/truth labels withheld, 153 hybrid top-10 queries retrieved at least one labeled-relevant memory for 116 queries (75.8%), but returned zero relevant memories for 37 (24.2%). Only 46 queries (30.1%) placed relevant evidence at rank 1. Mean relevant hits per query was 1.183 and the median was 1. Mean raw recall@10 was 0.219; correcting for the top-10 ceiling on queries with more than 10 relevant records produced a nearly identical mean of 0.2243. Category mean recall ranged only from 0.155 (forced choice, n=3) to 0.231 (current state, n=25). This supports a narrow conclusion: the retrieval layer frequently gives downstream reasoning an incomplete or empty evidence set. It does not by itself establish whether an answer-generating model would be correct.

title: Experiment 05: API abstention decisions were inverted relative to benchmark expectations
detail: All three queries labeled should_abstain=true returned api_abstain=false. Conversely, api_abstain=true appeared on 9 queries whose benchmark label was should_abstain=false, including the straightforward question 'What is T-4's rated generator capacity?' and queries with relevant evidence in the returned top 10. Thus this run produced 0/3 required abstentions and 9 apparent false abstentions. This finding uses the API's returned abstain boolean only; it does not infer abstention from empty relevant sets.

title: Experiment 05: a small set of records dominated results across heterogeneous queries
detail: Across 1,523 mapped result positions from 153 queries, one investigation report (e05m_0040) appeared in 98 queries, a technical note (e05m_0153) in 93, another investigation report (e05m_0029) in 85, and an overgeneralized executive summary (e05m_0038) in 71. The four records therefore appeared in 46%-64% of all query result sets despite heterogeneous query categories and claims. This concentration is consistent with a broad-document or importance reranking bias, but the mechanism is not proven. Follow-up should compare semantic-only search and inspect score components before attributing causality.

title: Experiment 05: semantic-only search does not materially fix incomplete evidence retrieval
detail: A paired 153-query rerun against POST /search, holding namespace, corpus, query order, and top_k=10 constant, improved mean raw recall@10 only from 0.2190 to 0.2265 (+0.00752). Recall was unchanged on 145/153 queries, better on 7, and worse on 1. Semantic-only reduced complete misses from 37 to 35 and increased relevant-at-rank-1 from 46 to 51. It rescued three hybrid misses (e05q_055, e05q_131, e05q_150) but created one new miss (e05q_098). Therefore the incomplete evidence view is largely shared by both endpoints rather than being explained solely by hybrid reranking.

title: Experiment 05: semantic and hybrid endpoints return highly overlapping result sets and similar latency
detail: Semantic-only and hybrid returned exactly the same ordered results for 102/153 queries and the same unordered result set for 106/153. Mean result-set Jaccard overlap was 0.9088 and median overlap was 1.0. Mean latency was similar: 12,096 ms for semantic-only versus 12,265 ms for hybrid; p95 was 13,684 ms versus 13,594 ms. Ranking concentration also persisted: e05m_0040 appeared in 98 semantic queries (also 98 hybrid), e05m_0153 in 95 semantic versus 93 hybrid, and e05m_0029 in 85 for both. This suggests substantial shared candidate generation or ranking behavior, but does not prove an internal implementation relationship. POST /search omitted the abstain field entirely, unlike /search/hybrid.
